3.4.1.3-f103.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.14, has 'nullius addictus', said of himself. Burton's plural fits his 'they' who follow only their own spirit.

3.4.1.3-f106.accuracy_reason: Tertullian, De praescriptione haereticorum 38 reads 'ad materiam suam caedem scripturarum confecit' about Marcion's sword rather than pen. The note quotes it correctly, and Burton's change to the plural is described accurately.

3.4.1.3-f110.accuracy_reason: Eon de l'Étoile (Eudo de Stella) was a twelfth-century Breton heretic. William of Newburgh, cited in Burton's sidenote, reports that he claimed divine status.

3.4.1.3-f118.accuracy_reason: The Lucilius fragment is preserved in Lactantius, Divine Institutes 1.22, and Book 1 is titled De falsa religione. The note is right that the sidenote's locus is Lactantius'.

3.4.1.3-f120.accuracy_reason: This is Persius, Prologue 8–11: 'quis expedivit psittaco suum χαῖρε … magister artis ingenique largitor venter'. Reading the belly as gain fits how Burton applies the line.

3.4.1.3-f132.accuracy_reason: Machiavelli argues in Discourses II.2 that Christianity has made men weak. The claim about where the Latin wording comes from is suitably hedged.

3.4.1.3-f134.accuracy_reason: 'Imaginatio laesa' is the standard term in Renaissance medicine for the damaged faculty that produces melancholy delusions.

3.4.1.3-f166.accuracy_reason: Febris was a Roman goddess of fever with several temples in Rome (Valerius Maximus 2.5.6). Most Roman fevers were malarial, so 'malaria' is acceptable.

3.4.1.3-f178.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.8 opens 'Olim truncus eram ficulnus, inutile lignum', spoken by a statue of Priapus that the carpenter chose to make a god.

3.4.1.3-f18.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 15.34–38 does have 'ardet adhuc, Ombos et Tentyra. summus utrimque' between these lines, and the standard text reads 'credat' and 'colit'.

3.4.1.3-f19.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 1.101 closes the Iphigenia passage, and 'religio' there means superstition or fear of the gods.

3.4.1.3-f20.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 1.6–7 is part of the opening lines on civil war.

3.4.1.3-f205.accuracy_reason: The definition of the limbus patrum is the standard theological one.

3.4.1.3-f215.accuracy_reason: Burton's 'propitius' echoes the people's prayer to the deified Romulus in Livy 1.16.3 ('volens propitius'), not Proculus's announcement (1.16.5–7). Calling the line a summary of Proculus's speech is too confident. That it is not Livy's exact wording is right.

3.4.1.3-f217.accuracy_reason: Herodotus 1.50 is right about the 3,000 of each kind of beast and the burned couches and cups. But those were destroyed. What went to Delphi was gold ingots cast afterwards plus other offerings, so 'the gifts were then sent on' is loose. Sardis as the place of the pyre is implied in Herodotus, not stated.

3.4.1.3-f218.accuracy_reason: Ammianus 25.4.17 gives the white oxen's greeting to Marcus Caesar with 'si iterum viceris, perimus'. Burton does drop 'iterum'.

3.4.1.3-f232.accuracy_reason: In Herodotus 1.47–48 the oracle names the tortoise and lamb that Croesus was boiling in a bronze cauldron.

3.4.1.3-f237.accuracy_reason: The limbus infantum was the limbo assigned to infants who died unbaptised.

3.4.1.3-f27.accuracy_reason: De carne Christi 5 reads 'credibile est, quia ineptum est'. Burton's version is the familiar paraphrase.

3.4.1.3-f30.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of 2 Cor 10:5 reads 'in captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi'.

3.4.1.3-f31.accuracy_reason: Ipse dixit (autos epha) was the formula by which Pythagoreans appealed to their master's authority.

3.4.1.3-f34.accuracy_reason: Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels, reads 'nec fides habet meritum, cui humana ratio praebet experimentum'.

3.4.1.3-f35.accuracy_reason: The saying 'Domine, si error est, a te ipso decepti sumus' is in Richard of St Victor, De Trinitate 1.2, which matches the sidenote.

3.4.1.3-f39.accuracy_reason: The jibe is traditionally attributed to Averroes, and the note hedges that attribution properly.

3.4.1.3-f40.accuracy_reason: The pyx and 'idem corpus numero' (numerical identity) are glossed correctly, and the framing matches what Burton says about Muslim and Jewish objections.

3.4.1.3-f43.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 15.10–11 reads 'quibus haec nascuntur in hortis / numina', and the satire mocks Egypt's worship of leeks and onions.

3.4.1.3-f45.accuracy_reason: 'Dii maiorum/minorum gentium' does come from the ranking of patrician houses as patres maiorum and minorum gentium, and it was applied to the greater and lesser gods.

3.4.1.3-f6.accuracy_reason: The episode is from Geoffrey of Monmouth, which is right. But the Merlin commentary printed under the name of Alanus de Insulis is of disputed authorship, probably not Alan of Lille's, and the note states it as his without a hedge.

3.4.1.3-f64.accuracy_reason: Lactantius (Div. Inst. 2.2) quotes Seneca on worshipping images while despising the craftsmen who made them.

3.4.1.3-f74.accuracy_reason: Ammianus (22.12) records that Julian was mocked as 'victimarius' for his many sacrifices, and the glosses of the two nicknames are correct.

3.4.1.3-f79.accuracy_reason: Branchidae is Didyma near Miletus, the site of Apollo's oracle and temple.

3.4.1.3-f82.accuracy_reason: Livy (8.9) has the Decii devoting themselves to the Di Manes and Tellus.

3.4.1.3-f89.accuracy_reason: 'Laethi' is a spelling of 'leti', and Propertius (3.13 in modern numbering) describes Eastern widows competing to die on their husband's pyre.
